content.body: Have you ever wondered how spell-checkers suggest corrections? They often calculate the 'edit distance' between words. Today, we'll learn a clever way to solve this using a lookup structure. We'll implement an algorithm that finds the minimum number of edits needed to transform one string into another.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Explain how a lookup structure helps avoid redundant calculations in edit distance.
• Implement the edit distance algorithm using a hash map (object) to store intermediate results.
• Apply the algorithm to calculate the minimum edits between two example strings.
content.title: What you'll learn
Try it
content.prompt: How many single-character edits (insert, delete, or replace) are needed to change 'cat' into 'bat'?

content.title: Try a longer pair
content.prompt: How many edits to change 'kitten' into 'sitting'?
content.successMessage: Great! You might have figured: 'k'→'s', 'e'→'i', and insert 'g' at the end.

content.title: One more
content.prompt: How many edits to change 'sunday' into 'saturday'?
content.successMessage: Nice! You checked possibilities: insert 'a' and 't', replace 'n'→'r'.

content.body: What you just did was mentally explore different edit paths. For longer words, manually checking all possibilities becomes overwhelming—like checking every pair in a large array.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When strings have 10+ characters, the number of possible edit sequences explodes. Checking them all is too slow. We need a smarter method that avoids redoing work. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Remember what we have already seen. Instead of recalculating edits for the same substrings over and over, we can store results in a lookup structure—like a notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step. This is the core of dynamic programming with a hash map.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll break the problem into smaller subproblems: the edit distance between prefixes of the two strings. We'll use a 2D structure (like a table) to store these distances, but we can implement it with a hash map keyed by string indices.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
For 'cat' and 'bat':
- Start with empty strings: distance 0.
- Build row by row: if letters match, take diagonal value; else, take 1 + min of left, top, diagonal.
- Final cell gives answer 1.
We avoid recomputing by storing each cell's value once.

content.body:
1. Create a lookup structure (object) keyed by 'i,j' string indices.
2. Initialize base cases: distance from empty string to prefixes.
3. Iterate through all i,j pairs:
   - If characters match, result = value at (i-1, j-1).
   - Else, result = 1 + min of three neighboring values.
4. Store each result in the lookup.
5. Return the value for full strings.
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up function and base cases
steps.instruction: Create a function minDistance that takes two strings word1 and word2. Initialize an empty object dp to act as our lookup table. Then, set the base case: dp['0,0'] = 0 (distance between two empty strings).
steps.hint: The dp object will store values for key combinations like 'i,j'. Start with the simplest case.
steps.expectedOutcome: dp should have one key '0,0' with value 0.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the foundation for our lookup structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure dp is an object and you've added the base key-value pair.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's try again. Create an empty object called dp, then assign 0 to dp['0,0'].

steps.title: Initialize first row and column
steps.instruction: Now, fill in the base cases for when one string is empty. Use loops: for i from 1 to word1.length, set dp[i+',0'] = i (deleting i characters). Similarly, for j from 1 to word2.length, set dp['0,'+j] = j (inserting j characters).
steps.hint: These represent the cost of converting a prefix to an empty string (all deletions or insertions).
steps.expectedOutcome: dp should have keys for all i,0 and 0,j with appropriate values.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've set the boundaries of our lookup table.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Ensure you're adding both the row and column base cases.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: dp[i+',0'] = i for each i, and dp['0,'+j] = j for each j.

steps.title: Loop through all character pairs
steps.instruction: Next, nest two loops: outer i from 1 to word1.length, inner j from 1 to word2.length. Inside, check if word1[i-1] equals word2[j-1]. We'll fill in the logic in the next step.
steps.hint: We're iterating over every combination of prefixes. Use 1-indexed i,j to match our dp keys.
steps.expectedOutcome: The nested loops should run for each i and j pair.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Good! You've set up the iteration to process all subproblems.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check your loop conditions: i and j should start at 1 and go up to the string lengths.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use for loops: outer over i, inner over j, both from 1 to length inclusive.

steps.title: Compute and store each distance
steps.instruction: Inside the loops, compute the value for dp[i+','+j]. If characters match, set it to dp[(i-1)+','+(j-1)]. Otherwise, set it to 1 plus the minimum of three neighbors: left (dp[i+','+(j-1)]), top (dp[(i-1)+','+j]), and diagonal (dp[(i-1)+','+(j-1)]).
steps.hint: This is where we use our lookup to avoid recomputation: we retrieve stored values and store the new one.
steps.expectedOutcome: Each dp[i,j] should be correctly computed based on the recurrence relation.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You're building the lookup table efficiently.
steps.feedbackPartial: Double-check the three neighbors and the minimum calculation.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: if chars match, use diagonal; else, 1 + min(left, top, diagonal).

steps.title: Return the final result
steps.instruction: After the loops, return dp[word1.length+','+word2.length], which holds the edit distance for the full strings.
steps.hint: The answer is stored in the bottom-right corner of our conceptual table.
steps.expectedOutcome: The function should return the correct edit distance.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've implemented the full algorithm using a lookup structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost done. Make sure you're returning the value for the full lengths.
steps.feedbackWrong: Return dp with key formed from word1.length and word2.length.

content.body: Great job! You've implemented the edit distance algorithm using a hash map to remember subproblem results. Key takeaways: we store computed distances keyed by string indices to avoid redundant work, and we check the structure before recomputing. This 'remember what we have already seen' pattern is powerful for many dynamic programming problems.
